name: ldapsearch - Get Password Policy via LDAP
description: Queries the domain password policy via anonymous or authenticated LDAP. Retrieves attributes like lockout threshold, password history, and complexity settings from the domain object. Quick way to get lockout thresholds before attempting password spraying.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== LDAP PASSWORD POLICY ATTRIBUTES ===
  pwdHistoryLength           → how many previous passwords remembered
  lockoutThreshold           → failed attempts before lockout (0 = disabled)
  lockoutDuration            → duration of lockout (in 100-nanosecond intervals)
  lockoutObservationWindow   → window for failed attempt counter
  minPwdLength               → minimum password length
  pwdProperties              → complexity flags

=== CONVERTING LOCKOUT DURATION ===
AD stores time as 100-nanosecond intervals (negative for durations):
  -18000000000 = 30 minutes
  Divide by 10,000,000 to get seconds, then by 60 for minutes
  -18000000000 / 10000000 / 60 = 30 minutes

=== UNAUTHENTICATED vs AUTHENTICATED ===
Anonymous bind (-x with no credentials) often works if null sessions allowed.
For authenticated:
  ldapsearch -h <dc> -x -D 'CN=forend,CN=Users,DC=INLANEFREIGHT,DC=LOCAL' -W ...
  or: ldapsearch -H ldap://<dc> -b 'DC=INLANEFREIGHT,DC=LOCAL' -D 'user@domain' -W ...

=== BASE DN FORMAT ===
For INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL: DC=INLANEFREIGHT,DC=LOCAL
For LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL: DC=LOGISTICS,DC=INLANEFREIGHT,DC=LOCAL

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

defense.why_it_works: In Active Directory the default security descriptor grants the built-in 'Authenticated Users' group read access to nearly every directory object (users, groups, computers, GPOs, trusts) and their attributes. So any valid domain account — however low-privileged — can enumerate the whole directory over LDAP/SAMR without hitting access-denied, which is why this returns data without needing admin. The password-policy attributes on the domain object are readable, so a plain LDAP bind retrieves lockout/length before you spray.
defense.prerequisites: Valid domain credentials (any authenticated user) and network access to a DC (LDAP 389/636).
defense.impact: Lockout/complexity settings that make spraying safe.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1087.002] Broad/bulk LDAP queries to the DC (Event 4662 directory-service access; Microsoft Defender for Identity reconnaissance alerts); one host reading large swaths of the directory in a short window.
defense.artifacts: LDAP query for domain policy attributes.
defense.prevention: AD is readable by any authenticated user by design, so prevention is limited - focus on DETECTION (Defender for Identity, LDAP/SMB anomaly monitoring), least privilege, disabling anonymous/null sessions, and REDUCING what's exposed (remove unnecessary SPNs, descriptions with secrets, over-shared folders).
defense.evasion: Use built-in tools (net, AD module, dsquery) that blend with normal admin activity; throttle and scope collection; avoid the noisiest methods (full BloodHound sweeps, RID brute) where Defender for Identity is present.
defense.misconfiguration: The LDAP server (Active Directory domain controller) allows anonymous binds or null-credential binds, exposing the directory tree to unauthenticated queries. Even when full anonymous access is disabled, authenticated-but-low-privilege domain users can enumerate all users, groups, SPNs, and sensitive attributes (description fields containing passwords, LAPS passwords if ACLs are wrong) because AD's default read ACL is very permissive.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Anonymous LDAP bind allowed (old domain or misconfigured):
# Test: ldapsearch -H ldap://<dc> -x -b '' -s base  (no -D or -w)
# If returns results -> anonymous bind works

# AD attribute exposure to all authenticated users (default permissive ACL):
# All users can read: userPrincipalName, sAMAccountName, memberOf,
#   servicePrincipalName, description, pwdLastSet, adminCount
# Description field often contains passwords set by admins during provisioning
defense.secure_config:
# Disable LDAP anonymous binds on domain controllers:
# Registry (on each DC):
Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters' \
    -Name 'LDAPServerIntegrity' -Value 2  # require signing

# Force LDAPS (LDAP over TLS) — block plaintext LDAP:
# GPO: Domain Controller Security Policy
#   Network Security: LDAP client signing requirements = Require signing

# Audit AD attribute ACLs — check who can read sensitive attributes:
Get-ADObject (Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName -Properties nTSecurityDescriptor

# Remove passwords from description/info fields (audit quarterly):
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Description |
    Where-Object {$_.Description -match 'pass|pwd|password|temp'} |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, Description

# Enable LDAP channel binding (KB4520412):
# HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters
#   LdapEnforceChannelBinding = 2
